text.text: Run the company from here. Plan customers have a Next service due date, so routes fill themselves. Every visit goes on the Service visits board; every product applied is written in Application records, which is the record your state can ask to see. Sent and overdue invoices both count in a customer's Awaiting payment.

pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the route supervisor, the office manager and every technician.
What lives where
Customers
: homes and businesses with their plan, next service due date, property notes, what they owe and how many visits are open.
Service visits
: each visit, with the target pest, technician, date, price, product cost and margin.
Application records
: the legal record of every product applied, linked to the visit and to the product.
Products and equipment
: products with their EPA numbers, equipment and safety gear, and what to reorder.
Invoices
: plan bills and one-time treatments.
A visit from booking to paid
Plan customers show up on the Dashboard when they are due; one-time calls come in as
New request
The route supervisor sets the technician and the date and moves the visit to
Scheduled
. A technician can press
Assign to me
On site the technician inspects, treats and writes the application record before leaving.
Mark done
stamps the date. Update the customer's Next service due.
The office sends the invoice. Past due becomes
Overdue
; Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue together.
Mark paid
stamps the date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's route, callbacks
Every Thursday: plan next week's routes from Due soon
Every Friday: count products and check safety gear
Every month: callbacks by route, record spot checks, license expiry dates
Making it yours

Rename plans and work types to match your services, add your products with their EPA numbers, and delete the sample customers once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Safety first, every stop

Read the label before you mix, wear what it says to wear, and keep products locked in the truck. Note children, pets, fish tanks and gardens in the property notes, and choose baits over sprays indoors where you can.
Visits by status, revenue by treatment type and unpaid invoices.
Overdue service visits
My service visits
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Plan customers due in the next 14 days
Callbacks
Plan customers are the heart of a pest control business. A tight route lets one technician service 12 to 18 homes a day; a loose one does eight and burns the margin in fuel.
Setting up a plan customer
Set
Plan
on the customer: Quarterly, Monthly or Commercial.
After each service, set
Next service due
: about 90 days out for quarterly, 30 for monthly. The Dashboard lists everyone due in the next 14 days.
Write access and safety details in
Property notes
: gates, dogs, crawlspace access, children or pets that limit which products you use.
Building the week
Every Thursday the route supervisor opens the Due soon list and groups the customers by area.
Each technician gets one area per day. Commercial accounts with fixed times (restaurants after close, daycares before opening) go in first; homes fill around them.
Book each stop as a service visit with the work type and target pest.
Text customers the day before. Many do not need to be home for an exterior service; note that on the card once they confirm.
At each stop
Read the property notes and last visit's application record
Inspect before treating: what pest, how much, where it comes in
Treat only what the label allows, where the label allows it
Write the application record before leaving: product, amount, area, target, weather
Leave a service note or door hanger saying what you did and any re-entry time
Update
Next service due
Pricing a plan

Price a quarterly visit by drive time plus time on site plus product, then add margin. Plans earn their keep on volume and on free callbacks being rare. If callbacks on a route climb, the treatment or the interval is wrong, not the customer.
Example

On Thursday the supervisor sees nine homes due in the next two weeks, six of them on the west side. He books them on Tuesday for Chidi, with the daycare at 6:30 am first. Two customers text back that the gate will be unlocked; he notes it on their cards for next time.
Rain and wind
Exterior sprays are not applied in rain or wind above the label limit. Move the stop to the next dry day and write the reason on the visit. Indoor and bait work goes ahead.
In most states every pesticide application must be recorded and kept for at least two years. A good record also protects you when a customer asks what was used around their children or pets.
What every application record holds
Service visit
and the customer it was for
Product
used, with its EPA registration number (kept on the product in Products and equipment)
Amount applied
: finished gallons, grams of gel, number of bait blocks
Target pest
and
Areas treated
, specific enough that another technician could find them
Weather
for exterior work: sky, temperature and wind
Applied on
, the date
The technician's name and license number, kept on the team member
Writing it well
Write it on site, before leaving, from the label, not from memory.
Name places: "under the dish machine and along the cook line," not "kitchen."
For bait stations, give the station numbers. Commercial customers keep a station map; ask for a copy.
Record nothing applied as well: an inspection-only visit says so.
Customer requests

When a customer asks what was used, print or send the application record and the product label. Answer questions with the label in hand. Never say a product is "safe"; say what the label says about re-entry and pets.
Weekly review
The route supervisor spot-checks five records a week for completeness
Every visit marked done has at least one application record or an "inspection only" note
Products used match what left the shelf (the weekly count shows it)
Example

A daycare director asks what was used in the kitchen last month. The office opens the application records for that visit: gel bait, 12 grams, under the sink and behind the refrigerator, with the product's EPA number. The director gets the record and the label the same afternoon and renews the commercial plan.
Licenses and training

Every applicator's license number and expiry date sits on their team record. Trainees apply only under a licensed technician's supervision; the record names the licensed technician too. Schedule continuing education well before licenses expire.
On a plan, a callback is free and quick: it is how you keep the customer. Too many callbacks on one route is a sign to look at the treatment, not to stop answering the phone.
When the customer calls
Ask what they are seeing, where, and how many. Ask for a photo; many "roaches" are beetles that wandered in.
Check their plan and the last visit's application record.
Plan customers: book a callback within two working days at no charge. Tick
Callback
on the new visit.
One-time customers: the warranty on the original job tells you whether it is free.
On the callback visit
Inspect first: find where the pests are coming from, not just where they are seen
Look for conditions: leaks, gaps under doors, food left out, mulch against the siding
Treat what the label allows; prefer baits indoors
Tell the customer which conditions they can fix, in writing
Write the application record
Complaints that are not about pests

Damage to plants, a stain on a floor, a technician who left a gate open: the owner or office manager calls back the same day, listens, and fixes it. A small credit or a free service costs far less than a lost plan.
Reviewing callbacks
Every month, open the Callbacks list on the Dashboard.
Many ant callbacks after the first spring rain: switch to baits on those routes before the season.
One technician with most callbacks: ride along for a day.
One property with repeated callbacks: a full inspection for conditions, with a written report for the customer.
Example

A homeowner texts a photo of ants in the bathroom ten days after an ant treatment. The office books a callback for the next morning. Chidi finds a trail coming through a gap at the tub drain, places gel bait along it, seals the gap, and shows the customer. The next quarterly visit notes no ants inside.
